extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers interested in F. Scott Fitzgerald and American literature
extracted.subtask_description: Summative critical appraisal of F. Scott Fitzgerald's life, artistic evolution, thematic concerns, and the reception of his novels and short stories over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics praised Fitzgerald's later works for improved form and construction and derided his earliest novel for its chaotic organization; reviewers highlighted that his early prose 'had almost every fault and deficiency that a novel can possibly have.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early failures: This Side of Paradise criticized for poor form and construction; improvement visible in The Beautiful and Damned and further refined in The Great Gatsby. Expect stronger novels to show disciplined organization, coherent structure, and elimination of earlier defects in prose and plotting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental style and originality
rubrics_metrics.description: This Side of Paradise was praised for its experimental style — unspooling plot via textual fragments, letters, and poetry — and contemporaries declared the work 'pulsed with originality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality can be manifested as formal experimentation (mixed genres, non-linear fragments). Anti-pattern: experimentation that results in incoherence or off-putting malapropisms that irritate editors and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose as lyric / natural sentence craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald believed prose has a basis in lyric verse and originally crafted sentences by ear; over time he mastered writing in 'natural sentences' and refined his prose style toward lyrical, polished phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sentence-level qualities: rhythm, lyricism, ear for language. Praise (Gertrude Stein) emphasized his ability to write in natural sentences; weakness included earlier malapropisms and descriptive non sequiturs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative economy and polish
rubrics_metrics.description: The Great Gatsby was singled out as 'compact, economical, polished in the technique of the novel,' marking a movement from improvisation to conscientious craftsmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality work demonstrates economy of language, tightness of narrative, and careful polishing. Anti-pattern: sprawling, indulgent passages that could have been tightened without loss of effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discernible progression and maturity across novels
rubrics_metrics.description: Each successive novel represented a discernible progression in literary quality and artistic maturity, moving from a brilliant improviser toward a painstaking artist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess an author's oeuvre for growth: improved technique, deeper thematic insight, greater control of form. Examples: improvement from This Side of Paradise → The Beautiful and Damned → The Great Gatsby.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short stories: commercial tailoring vs artistic coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald's 164 short stories are often judged inferior to his novels because money became his primary impetus; he tailored stories to magazine tastes (young love, saccharine denouements) and thus many works lacked thematic coherence and quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating short fiction, beware of stories written primarily for market demands—signs include predictable sentimental endings, formulaic plots, and loss of authorial ambition. Value steadiness of theme and artistic integrity over purely commercial appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of generational zeitgeist (Jazz Age chronicling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald was widely hailed as the chronicler of the Jazz Age — vividly portraying a generation 'dedicated more than the last to the fear of poverty and the worship of success' — and his works turned national attention to that cohort's attitudes and lifestyle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how effectively fiction captures and interprets a historical or generational moment: authenticity of details, persuasive social portrait, and capacity to shape public perception. Anti-pattern: superficial period trappings without deeper insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of wealth, class, and the leisure class
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurrent theme is the psychic and moral gulf between average Americans and wealthy elites; Fitzgerald satirized the leisure class and explored class permanence and barriers to social mobility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate portrayal of class: does the work illuminate structural inequalities, social attitudes of the wealthy, and limits of the American dream? Mencken's critique warns that an exclusive focus on the rich can reduce broader relevance, but sustained, lucid satire of elites can yield timeless social documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Otherness and outsider perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Many characters (notably Jay Gatsby) are defined by 'otherness' — obscure origins, indeterminate status — reflecting Fitzgerald's own outsider experience; this perspective captures perennial American anxieties about status and belonging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess characterization for credible outsider perspectives: convincingly rendered social exclusion, ambiguous identities, and the narrative consequences of being an outsider. Strength: universal resonance; anti-pattern: reducing otherness to caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alleged vacuity / engagement with socio-political ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: A common criticism was that Fitzgerald's fiction 'lacked engagement with the salient socio-political issues of his time' and that he had 'few ideas to express,' evidence of perceived intellectual vacuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging intellectual substance, consider whether fiction engages broader social/political questions or remains narrowly aesthetic. Note Fitzgerald's own stance that he wrote for a largely apolitical generation; absence of politics may be defensible as period realism but can also be judged as shallow by some critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriative tendency (use of others' private materials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald frequently drew on private correspondence, diary entries, and others' life experiences in his fiction — for example, quoting verbatim letters he had received — which drew ethical and critical notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ethical and artistic implications of using real people's private materials: consider consent, transformation into fiction, and whether the appropriation serves a compelling artistic purpose or feels exploitative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical reevaluation and measures of lasting significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitzgerald's reputation underwent posthumous reevaluation: The Great Gatsby gained popularity (distribution in Armed Services Editions, later high sales), entered school curricula, and came to be hailed as a masterwork and emblematic American novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess long-term significance by metrics such as sustained sales, inclusion in education, critical reassessment, editorial interventions (posthumous editions), and cultural commemoration (societies, landmarks). Short-term reception may differ markedly from long-term stature.
